label: IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS?
prompt: Click the service layer that best describes each scenario, based on how much of the stack the provider is managing for you.

items.task: You rent a virtual machine, then install and configure your own OS, database, and web server on it
items.explanation: The provider only manages the underlying hardware, virtualization, and networking. Everything from the OS up is your responsibility — the classic IaaS tradeoff.

items.task: You push your app's code to a platform, and it handles the OS, runtime, and scaling automatically
items.explanation: Platform as a Service manages the operating system and runtime for you. You only think about your application code — Heroku and Vercel work this way.

items.task: Your team uses a web-based email inbox and never installs, patches, or configures anything
items.explanation: A fully finished, ready-to-use application delivered over the internet is SaaS. Gmail is the textbook example — the provider manages the entire stack.

items.task: Your company sets up its own custom Linux server images on rented cloud hardware for full control over the OS
items.explanation: Custom OS images and full control over the operating system layer is the signature of IaaS — you get raw compute and decide everything above it.

items.task: Your team subscribes to a project management tool and just logs in through a browser to use it
items.explanation: No installation, no infrastructure decisions, just a finished product accessed through a browser — that's SaaS.

items.task: You deploy code with a single command, and the platform automatically provisions the runtime and scales instances under load
items.explanation: Automatic runtime provisioning and scaling based on your code, without managing servers yourself, is the core PaaS pitch.
